extraction.name: LAMBADA
extraction.description: LAMBADA (LAnguage Modeling Broadened to Account for Discourse Aspects) is a dataset to evaluate the capabilities of computational models for text understanding by means of a word prediction task. It is a collection of narrative passages sharing the characteristic that human subjects are able to guess their last word if they are exposed to the whole passage, but not if they only see the last sentence preceding the target word. To succeed on LAMBADA, computational models cannot simply rely on local context, but must be able to keep track of information in the broader discourse.
extraction.creator: Denis Paperno, Germán Kruszewski, Angeliki Lazaridou, Quan Ngoc Pham, Raffaella Bernardi, Sandro Pezzelle, Marco Baroni, Gemma Boleda, Raquel Fernández; CIMeC - Center for Mind/Brain Sciences, University of Trento; Institute for Logic, Language & Computation, University of Amsterdam
extraction.citeAs: Paperno, D., Kruszewski, G., Lazaridou, A., Pham, Q. N., Bernardi, R., Pezzelle, S., Baroni, M., Boleda, G., & Fernández, R. (2016). The LAMBADA dataset: Word prediction requiring a broad discourse context. arXiv:1606.06031.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Passages were sourced from the BookCorpus (unpublished novels). After duplicate removal and filtering out potentially offensive material, the corpus contained 5,325 novels and 465 million words. Novels were randomly divided into training and development+testing partitions. Passages were filtered using a combination of four language models to remove easy-to-predict items, then evaluated by human subjects via CrowdFlower crowdsourcing in a three-step pipeline: (1) one subject guessed the target word from the whole passage; (2) if correct, a second subject also guessed from the whole passage; (3) if also correct, additional subjects tried to guess from the target sentence only (up to 10 unsuccessful guesses required for inclusion). Only passages passing all steps were included.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Manual Human Curator, User-generated content data
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The BookCorpus (Zhu et al., 2015), a collection of unpublished novels containing 5,325 novels and 465 million words after duplicate removal and filtering of potentially offensive material.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Novels were randomly divided into equally-sized training and development+testing partitions. Passages were filtered using a combination of four language models (a pre-trained RNN and three models trained on the BookCorpus: a standard 4-gram model, a RNN, and a feed-forward model); any passage whose target word had probability above 0.00175 according to any of the language models was excluded. The remaining passages were then filtered through a three-step human crowdsourcing pipeline. About 84-86% of items were discarded at step 1, an additional 6-7% at step 2, and another 3-5% at step 3, resulting in approximately 1 in 25 input examples passing all selection steps.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Duplicate removal and filtering of potentially offensive material using a stop word list from the BookCorpus. Passages were constructed with a context of minimum complete sentences cumulatively containing at least 50 tokens before the target sentence. Automated filtering using four language models to exclude passages where the target word was easily predictable by standard language models (probability threshold of 0.00175). Vocabulary restricted to the 60K most frequent words in the training set.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Human subjects annotated passages via a three-step crowdsourcing pipeline on CrowdFlower: Step 1 - one subject guessed the target word given the whole passage (context + target sentence); Step 2 - if step 1 was correct, a second subject guessed the target word from the whole passage; Step 3 - if step 2 was also correct, additional subjects (up to 10) tried to guess the target word from the target sentence only (3 guesses allowed per subject). A passage was included in LAMBADA only if both steps 1 and 2 were successful and no subject in step 3 could guess the target word. Subjects were prevented from judging the same item in both passage and sentence conditions.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The strict hit-or-miss approach required two consecutive subjects to exactly match the missing word in the broad context, and no subject (out of ten) to provide it based on local context only (even with 3 guesses). Alternative designs (e.g., step 3 before step 2 or step 1) were found to be more expensive. The approach of including passages where broad-context subjects provided synonymous continuations was considered but rejected as practically and methodologically challenging.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: At least 2 subjects for broad-context guessing (steps 1 and 2), plus up to 10 subjects for sentence-only guessing (step 3). Each item cost $1.24 on average.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Four language models used for automated filtering: a pre-trained RNN (Mikolov et al., 2011), a standard 4-gram model trained on BookCorpus, an RNN trained on BookCorpus, and a feed-forward model trained on BookCorpus. POS tagging was used for dataset analysis.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The development set of LAMBADA, along with the training corpus, is available for download at http://clic.cimec.unitn.it/lambada/. The test set was to be made available at the time of a planned public competition. No further versioning or deprecation policy is described.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: LAMBADA is intended to encourage the development of new computational models capable of genuine understanding of broad context in natural language text, promoting progress in language understanding research.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Proper nouns are hugely overrepresented in LAMBADA (48% of target words), while other categories (verbs, adjectives, adverbs) are underrepresented compared to the input data distribution. More than 80% of LAMBADA passages include the target word in the context. LAMBADA items contain quoted direct speech significantly more often than the input items overall (71% vs. 61%). The dataset is biased toward passages that are difficult for standard language models by design, as one of the first filters excluded passages where language models could easily predict the target word.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: LAMBADA was designed to challenge language models with harder-than-average examples where broad context understanding is crucial, so standard language models are bound to fail on it by design. The dataset is sourced exclusively from unpublished novels (BookCorpus), limiting generalization to other text genres. The strict hit-or-miss annotation approach may exclude valid synonymous or paraphrastic answers. Cost considerations precluded using more subjects at stage 1, which could in principle improve filtering quality. The dataset is not intended for developing ad-hoc models only meant to predict the final word in LAMBADA-style passages.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Testing/benchmarking computational models for broad discourse context understanding via word prediction. The development set can be used to fine-tune models to the specifics of LAMBADA passages. Models should be trained on the provided training corpus (raw text from 2,662 novels, 203 million words) using unsupervised language modeling objectives. LAMBADA is proposed as a challenging test set to encourage development of new models capable of genuine understanding of broad context in natural language text.
